lesson.title: Lines a Graph Can Approach but Never Touch: Understanding Asymptotes
lesson.summary: An asymptote is a line that a function's graph gets arbitrarily close to, arising whenever a function has an infinite limit or a limit at infinity, and this single idea branches into the vertical, horizontal, and oblique cases studied next.
lesson.body:
Continuity describes where a function behaves well. Asymptotes describe what happens at the edges of that good behavior, either at a specific input value where the function blows up, or far out toward positive or negative infinity where the function's values may settle into a pattern. Both situations are captured by a single general idea: an asymptote is a straight line that the graph of a function gets arbitrarily close to, without necessarily ever touching it.

There are two different circumstances that produce an asymptote, and they correspond to two different kinds of limits. When the limit of f(x) as x approaches some finite value a is infinite, either positive or negative infinity, the vertical line x = a is called a vertical asymptote. This situation is exactly what happens at an infinite discontinuity, the kind of break where cancellation is not possible and the function genuinely diverges. Separately, when the limit of f(x) as x approaches positive or negative infinity settles to some finite number L, the horizontal line y = L is called a horizontal asymptote. A third, related case, the oblique or slant asymptote, occurs when the graph approaches a non-horizontal line as x runs off to infinity.

A more general definition ties these together: a line is an asymptote of the graph of f if the vertical or perpendicular distance between the graph and that line shrinks toward 0 as the point on the graph moves further out, either as x approaches a fixed value a from one side, in the vertical case, or as x itself grows without bound, in the horizontal and oblique cases.

The simplest and most iconic example is f(x) = 1/x. Near x = 0, testing values from the right, x = 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 give f(x) = 10, 100, and 1000, growing without bound, so the limit of 1/x as x approaches 0 from the right is positive infinity. Testing from the left, x = -0.1 and -0.01 give f(x) = -10 and -100, so the limit from the left is negative infinity. This infinite behavior at x = 0 means the vertical line x = 0 is a vertical asymptote. Meanwhile, as x grows large in either direction, 1/x shrinks toward 0: at x = 1000, f(x) = 0.001, and at x = -1000, f(x) = -0.001. So the horizontal line y = 0, the x-axis itself, is a horizontal asymptote in both directions, and the graph of 1/x famously hugs both axes without ever crossing them.

Because asymptotic behavior comes in genuinely different flavors depending on whether the input is fixed near a specific value or running off toward infinity, the next few sections treat each type separately: vertical asymptotes, which arise from infinite discontinuities at a fixed input; horizontal asymptotes and oblique asymptotes, which arise from limits at infinity; each with precise algebraic tests built on the polynomial and rational function tools already covered.
